method: Rebuild from primary text. Labor Code Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 1, Article 1 (§§200-209) was fetched in full from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and read as a whole, which is how §§201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.7, 201.9, 202 and 203 relate to one another; the article view was used because it shows the operative text of every section without the multi-version chooser. The construing case law was located through CourtListener. Assertions describe the REBUILT body.
queries: Cal. Lab. Code §§200-209 full text (leginfo, article view)
Naranjo Spectrum Security premium pay wages section 203 226 meal period
Naranjo 2024 good faith willful section 203 waiting time

assertions.text: wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due and payable immediately
an employee who quits is paid within 72 hours, or at the time of quitting if they gave 72 hours' previous notice
assertions.note: §202(a). The previous body said an employee who resigns with notice 'must be paid on their last day'; the section says 'at the time of quitting', which is the same day but is a moment, not a day.

assertions.text: an employee who quits without 72 hours' notice may request payment by mail, and the date of mailing is the date of payment
assertions.note: §202(a), final two sentences. Absent from the previous body. It is the provision that decides whether a payment was late.

assertions.text: a seasonal layoff in the curing, canning or drying of perishable fruit, fish or vegetables is payable within a reasonable time not exceeding 72 hours
assertions.note: §201(a), second sentence, with the mail proviso.

assertions.text: an oil drilling layoff is payable within a reasonable time not exceeding 24 hours excluding Saturdays, Sundays and holidays
assertions.note: §201.7, verbatim. Note the exclusion of weekends and holidays, which the previous defect note recorded but the body did not.

assertions.text: temporary services, motion picture, print shoot and live theatrical or concert venue employees are on separate schedules in §§201.3, 201.5, 201.6 and 201.9
assertions.note: The existence and subject of these sections was read from the article listing and from §203(a), which lists §§201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202 and 205.5 as the provisions whose breach triggers the penalty. Their operative deadlines were NOT read in full — see gaps. The clause names them rather than stating their rules, deliberately.

assertions.text: a wilful failure to pay makes the wages continue as a penalty at the same rate until paid or until an action is commenced, for no more than 30 days
assertions.note: §203(a), verbatim: 'If an employer wilfully fails to pay ... the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days.' The previous body said 'Late final pay accrues a waiting time penalty of one day of wages per day late, up to thirty (30) days' — it dropped 'wilfully', and it dropped that filing suit stops the clock.

assertions.text: an employer that reasonably and in good faith disputes that the wages are due has not acted wilfully
assertions.note: Naranjo (2024), quoted below, describing this as long established law and citing In re Trombley (1948) 31 Cal.2d 801, Barnhill v. Robert Saunders & Co. (1981) 125 Cal.App.3d 1 and 8 C.C.R. §13520. This is the single most consequential thing the previous body did not have: it told a small employer that lateness alone creates a thirty-day penalty.

assertions.text: an employee who secretes or absents themselves to avoid payment, or refuses a full tender, takes no benefit for that time
assertions.note: §203(a), second sentence. Absent from the previous body.

assertions.text: meal and rest period premium pay is a wage that must be paid on the §§201-202 schedule
assertions.note: Naranjo (2022), quoted below. The previous body's final pay list was wages plus accrued vacation; premium pay is the item most likely to be missed, because payroll does not think of it as a wage.

priorDefects: contradicted: 'Late final pay accrues a waiting time penalty of one day of wages per day late, up to thirty (30) days.' §203(a) conditions the penalty on a WILFUL failure, and a reasonable good faith dispute defeats wilfulness. Stated as written, the clause tells an employer it owes thirty days' pay for a payroll timing error it disputes in good faith.
omitted: that commencing an action stops the penalty running (§203(a)).
omitted: that an employee who avoids payment or refuses a full tender loses the benefit (§203(a)).
omitted: the mail election in §202(a) and its effect on when payment is treated as made.
omitted: the oil drilling deadline in §201.7 and the exclusion of weekends and holidays.
omitted: §§201.3, 201.5, 201.6 and 201.9, all of which §203(a) itself lists.
omitted: that meal and rest premium pay is a wage for these purposes (Naranjo 2022).
gaps: The deadlines in §§201.3 (temporary services), 201.5 (motion picture), 201.6 (print shoot) and 201.9 (live theatrical and concert venue) were not read in full. The rebuilt clause names those sections and says they govern, which is accurate and incomplete: a temporary staffing agency reading this clause learns that it is on a different clock and not what that clock is.

8 C.C.R. §13520 is the regulation that defines a good faith dispute, and Naranjo cites it. It could not be read: the publisher of the California Code of Regulations, govt.westlaw.com, returns HTTP 403 at this environment's egress proxy. The rebuilt clause therefore states that a good faith dispute defeats wilfulness without stating what makes a dispute good faith, and a reader could take more comfort from that than the regulation allows.
Whether the §203 penalty is computed on a calendar-day or working-day basis was not researched, and the rebuilt clause says 'the same daily rate' without resolving it.

§201(b)-(d) and §202(b)-(d) contain a deferral and retirement-plan-contribution scheme for state employees. It was read and deliberately not carried, on the assumption that no user of this corpus is the State of California.

judicialQuotations.case: Naranjo v. Spectrum Security Services, Inc. (Cal. 2024)
judicialQuotations.quote: Under long established law, an employer cannot incur civil or criminal penalties for the willful nonpayment of wages when the employer reasonably and in good faith disputes that wages are due.

judicialQuotations.case: Naranjo v. Spectrum Security Services, Inc. (Cal. 2022) 13 Cal.5th 93
judicialQuotations.quote: The Court of Appeal was correct that premium pay is a statutory remedy for a legal violation. But the court's further conclusion that premium pay cannot constitute wages rests on a false dichotomy: that a payment must be either a legal remedy or wages. For these purposes, section 226.7 is both.

note: The two Naranjo decisions pull in opposite directions for an employer and the clause has to carry both. The 2022 decision widens what must be paid on the §§201-202 clock; the 2024 decision narrows when failing to pay it is penalised. A clause that carried only the first would overstate the exposure and a clause that carried only the second would understate the duty.
